title: 여기 밥 맛있어  (The Food Here Is Delicious)

segments.t: At noon in the KBS staff cafeteria, Kim Tae-ho hands out lunch coupons and boasts that passing pop stars all know him well. Listen for the expressions for 'the food is delicious' and 'I had no idea'.
사람 모이면 귀찮으니까 조용히 밥이나 먹자.
Let's savour each line of this cafeteria lunch.

'These are four thousand won apiece.' Holding up a paper meal ticket, Tae-ho states the price per ticket: 'for one', followed by 'four thousand', with a suffix tacked onto the price to add the sense of 'each' or 'apiece' This means that.

'The food here is delicious.' Three short words you can use at any good lunch spot: 'here', the word for cooked rice (and by extension a whole meal), and 'tastes great'. Add a polite ending to use it with strangers We built from this.

'May I eat two of these?' Reaching for side dishes, Seung-chan counts 'two items' plus the suffix for 'each'. Any action followed by the permission-asking ending is the classic Korean way to ask 'may I...?' or 'is it okay if I...?' It is a handy word.

'Go ahead and eat!' Tae-ho grants permission with one casual form of the word 'to eat'. Between friends or from a senior to a junior, that bare spoken form doubles as both 'eat!' and 'sure, help yourself!' It is a handy word.
사람 모이면 귀찮으니까 조용히 밥이나 먹자.

'It's a hassle if a crowd gathers, so let's just eat quietly.' Spotting famous singers across the room, Tae-ho pretends fans will mob him, explaining 'because it is bothersome', then saying 'quietly' and suggesting 'let's just eat our meal' The word doubles the.

'Are you close with them?' Impressed, Seung-chan asks a question built on the word 'to be close friends'. Inserting an honorific infix honours his boss, while the formal question ending keeps the rookie's tone respectful This literally means that.

'Oh, close doesn't even cover it!' Tae-ho brags by literally asking 'is it merely being close?' — a lively idiom meaning 'way more than just close!'. You will hear that emphatic ending whenever someone exaggerates how obvious something is This means that.

'They didn't know him at all.' Here comes the punchline: the word for 'not at all' teams up with the past word of the word 'to not know'. Pair that word with a negative whenever you want 'zero clue' Notice the word for. Now let's listen to the whole cafeteria scene from top to bottom.
사람 모이면 귀찮으니까 조용히 밥이나 먹자.
With phrases for praising the food, asking permission to eat, and saying someone had no idea at all, you are ready for lunch and office tall tales alike. See you after lunch!

lines.fragment: 사람 모이고 그러면 귀찮으니까 조용히 밥이나 먹자
